title: Part 2, Chapter 5
paragraphs: This was a gentleman no longer young, stiff and portly in appearance, with a cautious, sour expression. He began by stopping short in the doorway and staring around with open, offensive astonishment, as though asking himself what kind of place he had come to. With deliberate mistrust, and with an air of being alarmed and almost insulted, he surveyed Raskolnikov's low, cramped little room. With the same amazement he stared at Raskolnikov himself, lying on his wretched dirty sofa, undressed, disheveled, unwashed, looking fixedly back at him. Then with equal deliberation he examined the rough, unkempt figure and unshaven face of Razumihin, who stared him boldly in the eye without getting up. An awkward silence lasted a couple of minutes, and then, as might have been expected, there was a shift in the atmosphere. Judging, probably from certain unmistakable signs, that he would get nowhere in this cramped little room by trying to intimidate them, the gentleman softened slightly. He addressed Zossimov in a polite but stern voice, emphasizing every syllable:
"Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a student, or formerly a student?"
Zossimov shifted slightly, and would have answered, had Razumihin not beaten him to it.
"Here he is, lying on the sofa! What do you want?"
This blunt "what do you want" seemed to cut the ground from under the pompous gentleman's feet. He began turning toward Razumihin, but checked himself in time and turned back to Zossimov.

"This is Raskolnikov," Zossimov mumbled, nodding in his direction. Then he gave a prolonged yawn, opening his mouth as wide as it would go. After that he lazily reached into his waistcoat pocket, pulled out a huge gold pocket watch in a round hunter's case, opened it, glanced at it, and just as slowly and lazily put it back.

Raskolnikov himself lay silent, on his back, staring persistently, though without comprehension, at the stranger. Now that his face was turned away from the strange flower on the wallpaper, it was extremely pale and wore a look of anguish, as though he had just undergone a painful operation or been released from the rack. But the newcomer gradually began to catch his attention, then his curiosity, then his suspicion, and finally his alarm. When Zossimov said "This is Raskolnikov," he quickly sat up on the sofa and in an almost defiant but weak, breaking voice said:
"Yes, I am Raskolnikov! What do you want?"
The visitor studied him and pronounced impressively:
"Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin. I believe I have reason to hope that my name is not entirely unknown to you?"
But Raskolnikov, who had been expecting something completely different, stared at him blankly, as though he were hearing the name Pyotr Petrovitch for the first time.
"Is it possible that you have not yet received any information?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, somewhat put out.

In reply, Raskolnikov sank languidly back onto the pillow, put his hands behind his head, and stared at the ceiling. A look of dismay crossed Luzhin's face. Zossimov and Razumihin studied him with even greater curiosity, and at last he showed unmistakable signs of embarrassment.
"I had assumed and calculated," he faltered, "that a letter posted more than ten days ago, perhaps even two weeks..."

"Look, why are you standing in the doorway?" Razumihin broke in. "If you have something to say, sit down. You and Nastasya are crowding the place. Nastasya, make room. Here is a chair -- thread your way in!"

He pushed his chair back from the table, making a little space between the table and his knees, and waited in a rather cramped position for the visitor to "thread his way in." The moment was chosen so that refusal was impossible, and the visitor squeezed through, hurrying and stumbling. Reaching the chair, he sat down and looked suspiciously at Razumihin.

"No need to be nervous," Razumihin blurted out. "Rodya has been sick for five days, delirious for three, but he is recovering now and has an appetite. This is his doctor, who just examined him. I am a friend of Rodya's, also a former student, and right now I am taking care of him. So do not mind us -- just go on with your business."
"Thank you. But will my presence and conversation not disturb the patient?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, turning to Zossimov.
"N-no," Zossimov mumbled. "You might even entertain him." He yawned again.

"He has been conscious for a while now, since morning," Razumihin continued, whose easy familiarity seemed like such natural good nature that Pyotr Petrovitch began to relax a little -- partly, perhaps, because this shabby, impudent young man had introduced himself as a student.
"Your mother --" Luzhin began.
"Hmm!" Razumihin cleared his throat loudly. Luzhin looked at him inquiringly.
"Never mind, go on."
Luzhin shrugged.

"Your mother had begun a letter to you while I was staying in her area. Upon arriving here, I deliberately waited a few days before visiting, so that I could be entirely certain you had been informed. But now, to my astonishment..."
"I know, I know!" Raskolnikov cried out with sudden impatient irritation. "So you are the _fiance_? I know, and that is enough!"
Pyotr Petrovitch was clearly offended this time, but said nothing. He made a violent effort to understand what was happening. There was a moment's silence.

Meanwhile Raskolnikov, who had half turned toward him when he answered, was now staring at him with marked curiosity, as though he had not gotten a good look at him before, or as though something new had struck him. He even sat up on purpose to study him. There was certainly something peculiar about Pyotr Petrovitch's whole appearance -- something that seemed to justify the title of "fiance" so unceremoniously applied to him. First, it was evident -- far too evident -- that Pyotr Petrovitch had made eager use of his days in the capital to spruce himself up in anticipation of his bride -- a perfectly innocent undertaking. Even his own somewhat smug awareness of how much better he looked might have been forgiven under the circumstances, given that he had assumed the role of fiance. All his clothes were fresh from the tailor and perfectly fine, except for being too new and too obviously meant to impress. Even the stylish new round hat carried the same significance. Pyotr Petrovitch treated it with excessive respect, holding it too carefully in his hands. The exquisite pair of lavender gloves -- real Louvain -- told the same story, if only because he did not wear them but carried them for show. Light, youthful colors dominated his outfit. He wore a charming summer jacket in fawn, light trousers, a matching waistcoat, crisp new linen, and a cravat of the lightest cambric with pink stripes -- and the best part was that it all suited him. His fresh, even handsome face looked younger than his forty-five years. His dark mutton-chop whiskers framed both sides nicely, growing thick on his shining, clean-shaven chin. Even his hair, touched here and there with grey and curled at a barber's, did not look ridiculous as curled hair usually does by making a man resemble a German at his own wedding. If there was something unpleasant and repulsive in his rather good-looking, imposing face, it came from entirely different causes. After this unceremonious inspection, Raskolnikov smiled maliciously, sank back onto the pillow, and stared at the ceiling as before.
But Mr. Luzhin steeled himself and seemed to decide to ignore their peculiarities.

"I am deeply sorry to find you in this condition," he began, breaking the silence with an effort. "Had I known of your illness, I would have come sooner. But you know how business is. I also have an important legal matter in the Senate, not to mention other concerns you can probably guess. I am expecting your mother and sister any minute."
Raskolnikov stirred and seemed about to speak; his face showed some excitement. Pyotr Petrovitch paused and waited, but as nothing followed, he went on:
"... Any minute. I have found lodgings for them upon their arrival."
"Where?" asked Raskolnikov weakly.
"Very close by, in Bakaleyev's house."
"That is on Voskresensky," Razumihin put in. "Two floors of rooms, rented out by a merchant named Yushin. I have been there."
"Yes, rooms..."

"A disgusting place -- filthy, stinking, and worse, of dubious reputation. Things have happened there, and all sorts of shady people live there. I went there about some scandalous business. It is cheap, though..."

"I could not, of course, have learned so much about it, being a stranger in Petersburg myself," Pyotr Petrovitch replied stiffly. "However, the two rooms are exceedingly clean, and since it is only for a short time... I have already found a permanent flat -- that is, our future home," he said, addressing Raskolnikov, "and I am having it renovated. Meanwhile, I myself am crammed into lodgings with my friend Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, in Madame Lippevechsel's apartment. It was he who told me about Bakaleyev's house."
"Lebeziatnikov?" said Raskolnikov slowly, as if trying to recall something.
"Yes, Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, a clerk in the Ministry. Do you know him?"
"Yes... no," Raskolnikov answered.

"Excuse me, I thought you did from your question. I was once his guardian.... A very nice young man, quite progressive. I like to meet young people -- one learns new things from them." Luzhin looked around at them all hopefully.
"In what way?" asked Razumihin.

"In the most serious and essential ways," Pyotr Petrovitch replied, as though delighted by the question. "You see, it has been ten years since I visited Petersburg. All the new ideas, reforms, and trends have reached us in the provinces, but to see them clearly one has to be in Petersburg. And it is my view that you learn the most by observing the younger generation. And I must confess, I am delighted..."
"By what?"
"That is a broad question. I may be mistaken, but I think I detect clearer thinking, more -- how shall I put it -- critical rigor, more practicality..."
"That is true," Zossimov remarked offhandedly.

"Nonsense! There is no practicality." Razumihin jumped on him. "Practicality is hard to come by -- it does not drop from the sky. And for the last two hundred years we have been cut off from all practical life. Ideas are fermenting, sure," he said, turning to Pyotr Petrovitch, "and there is a desire for good, though in a childish form. You might even find honesty, despite the swarms of scoundrels. But there is no practicality. Practicality wears sturdy shoes."

"I cannot agree," Pyotr Petrovitch replied with obvious pleasure. "Of course people get carried away and make mistakes, but one must be tolerant. Those mistakes are merely evidence of enthusiasm for the cause and of unfortunate external conditions. If little has been accomplished, the time has been short. Of means I will not speak. But in my personal view, something has already been achieved. New valuable ideas and new valuable works are circulating in place of our old dreamy, romantic authors. Literature is maturing. Many harmful prejudices have been rooted out and ridiculed.... In a word, we have cut ourselves off irrevocably from the past, and that, in my opinion, is a great thing..."
"He has memorized it to show off!" Raskolnikov muttered suddenly.
"What?" Pyotr Petrovitch asked, not catching his words, but he got no answer.
"That is all quite true," Zossimov hastened to agree.

"Is it not?" Pyotr Petrovitch continued, glancing affably at Zossimov. "You must admit," he went on, addressing Razumihin with a hint of triumph and condescension -- he nearly added "young man" -- "that there has been progress, or as they say now, advancement in the name of science and economic truth..."
"A cliche."

"No, not a cliche! If, for example, I was told in the past 'love thy neighbor,' what came of it?" Pyotr Petrovitch went on, perhaps with excessive haste. "It came to my tearing my coat in half to share with my neighbor, and we both ended up half-naked. As the Russian proverb says, 'Chase two hares and you will not catch one.' But science now tells us: love yourself above all, for everything in the world rests on self-interest. If you love yourself and manage your own affairs properly, your coat stays whole. Economic truth adds that the more private affairs are properly organized in society -- the more whole coats, so to speak -- the stronger its foundations and the better the common welfare is organized too. So by acquiring wealth solely for myself, I am, in a manner of speaking, acquiring for everyone, and helping to ensure my neighbor gets a bit more than a torn coat -- not through personal charity, but as a natural consequence of general progress. The idea is simple, but unfortunately it has been slow to reach us, blocked by idealism and sentimentality. And yet it would seem to require very little intelligence to grasp..."

"Excuse me, I have very little intelligence myself," Razumihin cut in sharply, "so let us drop it. I started this conversation with a purpose, but I have gotten so sick over the last three years of this chatter for its own sake, this endless stream of cliches, always the same ones, that I blush when other people talk like that. You are naturally eager to display your knowledge, and I do not blame you -- that is perfectly forgivable. I just wanted to find out what sort of man you are, because so many unscrupulous people have latched onto the progressive cause lately and distorted everything they touch for their own benefit that they have dragged the whole cause through the mud. That is enough!"
"Excuse me, sir," Luzhin said, offended, speaking with excessive dignity. "Are you suggesting, so unceremoniously, that I too--"
"Oh, my dear sir... how could I?... Come, that is enough," Razumihin concluded, and he turned abruptly to Zossimov to continue their previous conversation.
Pyotr Petrovitch had the good sense to accept the retraction. He decided to leave in another minute or two.
"I trust our acquaintance," he said, addressing Raskolnikov, "may, upon your recovery and given the circumstances of which you are aware, grow closer... Above all, I wish you a return to health..."
Raskolnikov did not even turn his head. Pyotr Petrovitch began getting up.
"One of her clients must have killed her," Zossimov declared with certainty.
"No doubt about it," agreed Razumihin. "Porfiry is not revealing his own theory, but he is examining everyone who left pledges with her."
"Examining them?" Raskolnikov asked aloud.
"Yes. What of it?"
"Nothing."
"How is he tracking them down?" asked Zossimov.
"Koch supplied some names. Other names were on the pledge wrappers, and some people have come forward on their own."
"It must have been a cunning, experienced criminal! Such boldness! Such nerve!"

"That is exactly what it was not!" Razumihin interjected. "That is what throws everyone off the track. I maintain that he is not cunning, not experienced, and this was probably his first crime! Assume he was a novice and it is obvious that only luck saved him -- and luck can do anything. He probably did not even anticipate the obstacles! And how did he go about it? He grabbed jewelry worth ten or twenty rubles, stuffing his pockets, and rummaged through the old woman's trunks and rags -- yet they found fifteen hundred rubles in cash, plus banknotes, in a box in the top drawer of the chest! He did not know how to rob; he only knew how to kill. It was his first crime, I am telling you -- he panicked. And he escaped not through skill but through sheer luck!"

"You are talking about the murder of the old pawnbroker, I believe?" Pyotr Petrovitch put in, addressing Zossimov. He was standing with hat and gloves in hand, ready to leave, but felt inclined to toss off a few more intellectual remarks. He was clearly eager to make a good impression, and his vanity overrode his prudence.
"Yes. You have heard about it?"
"Oh yes, living in the neighborhood."
"Do you know the details?"

"I cannot say that, but what interests me is a different aspect of the case -- the larger question, so to speak. Setting aside the fact that crime has been rising sharply among the lower classes in the last five years, not to mention the constant robberies and arsons -- what strikes me as strangest is that crime is increasing proportionally in the higher classes too. In one place you hear of a student robbing the mail on the highway. In another, people of good social standing forge banknotes. In Moscow an entire gang was caught forging lottery tickets, and one of the ringleaders was a university lecturer. Then our embassy secretary abroad was murdered for some obscure financial motive.... So if this old pawnbroker was murdered by someone from a higher social class -- since peasants do not pawn gold trinkets -- how do we explain this moral decay among the civilized part of society?"
"There have been many economic changes," Zossimov offered.
"How do we explain it?" Razumihin pounced. "It could be explained by our deep-rooted impracticality."
"What do you mean?"

"What did your Moscow lecturer say when they asked him why he was forging notes? 'Everybody else is getting rich one way or another, so I wanted to get rich quick too.' I do not remember the exact words, but the gist was that he wanted money for nothing, without waiting or working! We have gotten used to having everything handed to us, to walking on crutches, to having our food pre-chewed. And then the great moment came, and everybody showed their true colors."
[*] The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 is meant. --TRANSLATOR'S NOTE.
"But morality? And, so to speak, principles..."
"But why do you worry about it?" Raskolnikov cut in suddenly. "It follows from your own theory!"
"From my theory?"
"Follow your theory to its logical conclusion, and it turns out people may be killed..."
"Good heavens!" cried Luzhin.
"No, that is not right," Zossimov put in.
Raskolnikov lay there with a white face and twitching upper lip, breathing painfully.
"There is a limit to everything," Luzhin went on haughtily. "An economic idea is not an incitement to murder, and one need only suppose..."

"And is it true," Raskolnikov interrupted once more, his voice suddenly quivering with fury and a strange delight in provoking him, "is it true that you told your _fiancee_... within an hour of her acceptance, that what pleased you most... was that she was poor... because it is better to raise a wife from poverty so that you can have total control over her and reproach her for being your benefactress?"

"Good God!" Luzhin cried, furious and flushed with embarrassment. "To twist my words like this! Forgive me, but the report that has reached you -- or rather, been conveyed to you -- has no basis in fact, and I... suspect who... in a word, this arrow... your mother... She seemed to me, in other respects, despite her many excellent qualities, to have a somewhat romantic and exalted way of thinking.... But I was a thousand miles from imagining that she would misunderstand and distort things in such a fantastic way.... And indeed... indeed..."
"I tell you what," cried Raskolnikov, raising himself on the pillow and fixing his piercing, glittering eyes on him. "I tell you what."
"What?" Luzhin stood still, waiting with a defiant and offended expression. Silence lasted for several seconds.
"If you ever again... dare to mention a single word... about my mother... I will throw you down the stairs!"
"What is the matter with you?" cried Razumihin.

"So that is how it is?" Luzhin went pale and bit his lip. "Let me tell you, sir," he began deliberately, making every effort to control himself but breathing hard, "from the very first moment I saw that you were hostile toward me, but I stayed on purpose to learn more. I can forgive a great deal in a sick man and a relative, but after this... never."
"I am not sick," cried Raskolnikov.
"So much the worse..."
"Go to hell!"

But Luzhin was already leaving without finishing, squeezing between the table and chair. Razumihin stood up this time to let him pass. Without glancing at anyone, without even nodding to Zossimov -- who had been signaling him for some time to leave the patient alone -- he walked out, carefully lifting his hat to shoulder height to keep from crushing it as he stooped through the doorway. Even the curve of his spine seemed to express the terrible insult he had received.
"How could you -- how could you!" Razumihin said, shaking his head in bewilderment.

"Leave me alone -- leave me alone, all of you!" Raskolnikov cried in a frenzy. "Will you ever stop tormenting me? I am not afraid of you! I am not afraid of anyone, not anyone now! Get away from me! I want to be alone, alone, alone!"
"Come on," said Zossimov, nodding to Razumihin.
"But we cannot just leave him like this!"
"Come on," Zossimov repeated firmly, and he walked out. Razumihin thought for a moment, then ran after him.
"It could be worse to disobey him," Zossimov said on the stairs. "He must not be agitated."
"What is wrong with him?"

"If only he could get some kind of positive shock -- that is what he needs! At first he was better.... You know, he has something on his mind! Some fixed idea weighing on him.... I am very much afraid of that -- there must be something!"

"Perhaps it is that gentleman, Pyotr Petrovitch. From their conversation it sounds like he is going to marry Raskolnikov's sister, and that Raskolnikov got a letter about it just before falling ill...."

"Yes, damn the man -- he may have made everything worse. But have you noticed? Raskolnikov takes no interest in anything, does not respond to anything, except one subject that seems to agitate him -- the murder."
"Yes, yes," Razumihin agreed. "I noticed that too. He is interested, frightened even. It shook him the day he fell ill at the police station -- he fainted."
"Tell me more about that tonight and I will tell you something afterward. He interests me very much! I will go back and check on him in half an hour.... There will not be any inflammation, though."
"Thanks! And I will wait at Pashenka's in the meantime and keep watch through Nastasya...."
Raskolnikov, left alone, looked with impatience and misery at Nastasya, but she lingered.
"Will you have some tea now?" she asked.
"Later! I am sleepy! Leave me."
He turned sharply to the wall, and Nastasya went out.
